name: Skovfogedegen

location.address: Strandvejen, opposite the northern end of Bellevue Strand, Klampenborg (edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave)

access: Free, no ticket. Stands on public ground beside the road Strandvejen at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave (the royal deer park), opposite Bellevue Strand. Open at all times.
transport: Klampenborg is roughly 10.9 km north of central Copenhagen. S-train line C (Kystbanen) from Copenhagen Central to Klampenborg station, about 16-20 minutes, then about 8 minutes on foot north along Strandvejen to the tree.
verify_notes: Ancient hollow pedunculate oak (Stilk-Eg) at the edge of Jaegersborg Dyrehave, right beside Strandvejen in Klampenborg, opposite Bellevue Strand. Existed since around year 1200 per three independent, dated sources: Kristeligt Dagblad (national newspaper, article dated 2025), Historisk Atlas (historiskatlas.dk, a Danish historical-sites database), and Den Store Danske / lex.dk (Denmark's national encyclopedia). That puts it at roughly 800-850 years old today. The Danish Dendrological Society's own tree register (dendron.dk, Individual_ID=993) independently corroborates species and gives hard measurements: girth (omkreds) 10.42 m = 1042 cm, height 12.9 m, diameter 3.32 m, and a vitality note 'Levende, svag' (living, weak) from a 2010 field survey; the same register field-verified the tree's exact GPS position on 20-11-2008 at 55.77911N 12.58948E, which is the coordinate used here. The heartwood at the centre of the trunk has rotted away and the trunk is hollow, but the tree survives because water and nutrient transport happens in the growth layer just under the bark. The name comes from Johan Georg Weissler (1771-1854), a Catholic forest ranger (skovfoged) who used the hollow trunk as a private prayer chamber (bedekammer) in the early 1800s; the cavity was also once used to store peat. It is one of the thickest and most famous oaks in Dyrehaven, the historic royal deer park. A Wikimedia Commons photo dated March 2025 (photographer: Toxophilus) shows the tree standing in the same hollow-trunked condition, which is good recent evidence it is still alive; no news or forum mention found of it falling or being felled. One un-sourced web snippet puts the age at only about 500 years, but it could not be traced to a dated, named source and is outweighed by the three that agree on 'since around 1200'; noting it here rather than silently dropping it.

name: Klopstocks Eg
access: Free, no ticket. Stands right beside Prinsessestien, a public path through Lyngby Aamose along Molleaadalen. Legally protected (fredet) since 1956, with a memorial plaque added in 1984, so a public authority has long treated it as open ground for visitors.
transport: Kongens Lyngby is roughly 11.9 km northwest of central Copenhagen. S-train to Sorgenfri station (about 22-24 minutes from Copenhagen H), then about 15 minutes on foot west along Prinsessestien through Lyngby Aamose to the tree.
verify_notes: Old pedunculate oak (Stilk-Eg) on Prinsessestien beside Lyngby Aamose, named after the German poet Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock (1724-1803), who spent summers nearby at Gramlille, Lyngby Hovedgade 28, during his 1751-1771 stay in Denmark on invitation from Frederik V; it has also been called Monrads Eg after D.G. Monrad. Legally protected (fredet) in 1956; a memorial plaque was put up in 1984. A storm in 2013 broke off a large branch but the tree survived and is still standing. Two independent sources: Danish Wikipedia (citing the Lyngby-Taarbaek municipal archive's own history page, stadsarkivet.ltk.dk) and the Danish Dendrological Society's tree register (dendron.dk, Individual_ID=90), which gives girth 6.05 m (605 cm), diameter 1.93 m, a 'maximal alder' (maximum estimated age) of 800 years, status 'Levende' (living) as of a 2008 field report, and field-verified GPS position (09-04-2011) at 55.77890N 12.46699E, used here. monumentaltrees.com carries an independent corroborating record for the same tree at the same site (used only as a cross-check, per the standing rule). The register states the age as a maximum rather than a point estimate, so the estimate here is kept broad rather than sharpened to '800'. No news or forum report found of it having fallen or been felled since the 2013 storm damage; it remains a legally protected, signposted landmark on a well-used public walking route.

name: Englaenderegen

location.address: Jaegersborg Dyrehave, by Magasindammen, northeast of Eremitageslottet

access: Free, no ticket, and marked wheelchair-accessible on the Nature Agency's own listing. Stands in the open deer park of Jaegersborg Dyrehave, a public UNESCO-listed royal hunting landscape with no gates or opening hours beyond dusk closing for cars.
transport: Central Copenhagen to Dyrehaven's edge is roughly 12.6 km. S-train line C to Klampenborg station (about 16-20 minutes from Copenhagen Central), then a walk of roughly 35-40 minutes through the deer park, past Eremitageslottet, to reach Magasindammen; this tree sits deeper into the park than the entrance, so the walk-in is the honest, longer part of the trip.
verify_notes: Pedunculate oak (Stilk-Eg) beside Magasindammen (a pond) in Jaegersborg Dyrehave, the royal deer park north of Copenhagen, northeast of Eremitageslottet. Carries a well-documented 1807 legend: during the Napoleonic-era British siege of Copenhagen, two of Wellington's soldiers, tired of service, stole their regiment's pay chest and buried it beside a freestanding oak northeast of the Hermitage; they never returned for it, and one confessed on his deathbed to a priest. Treasure-hunters, including a search made at the request of Queen Victoria, have dug around the tree ever since without finding anything, which the Danish Dendrological Society's register credits with accidentally aerating the roots and saving a tree that was dying at the time. Two independent sources: the Danish Dendrological Society's own tree register (dendron.dk, Individual_ID=100), which gives girth 5.46 m (546 cm), diameter 1.74 m, status 'Levende' (living) as of a 2008 field report, and field-verified GPS position (13-04-2008) at 55.79592N 12.57400E, used here; and Naturstyrelsen (the Danish Nature Agency)'s own recreation-site listing at udinaturen.dk, an official government source independent of the dendrological society, which repeats the same 1807 story and confirms the site and its accessibility. monumentaltrees.com carries a matching record for cross-check only. Age: the register states a range of 240 to 360 years based on a formula published in the society's own yearbook (Holten, Dansk Dendrologisk Aarsskrift 26, 1998), explicitly noting the measurements are from 1995; add roughly 31 years to bring that current, hence the broadened 270-390 band used here rather than the flatter original figures. No news, forum or register update found reporting the tree fallen, felled or dead.
